metadata.title: 1993 Case 26
metadata.original_presentation: A 73-year-old man was admitted to the hospital with a diagnosis of a contained, ruptured aneurysm of the left femoral artery.

required.content: What is the patient's occupational history and exposure risks?
required.response: The patient was a retired shipyard pipe fitter, with known exposure to asbestos.

teaching_points.content: Occupational exposure to asbestos is a risk factor for various respiratory diseases and cancers.

required.content: What is the patient's smoking history?
required.response: He had smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 30 years and then switched to pipe-smoking 32 years before admission.

teaching_points.content: Long-term smoking is a significant risk factor for cardiovascular diseases and cancers.

required.content: What are the patient's past medical conditions and treatments?
required.response: The patient had chronic bronchitis managed with theophylline, hypertension treated with enalapril, and a history of stage B1 carcinoma of the prostate treated with radiation therapy. He also had a left hemicolectomy for carcinoma of the colon.

teaching_points.content: Chronic bronchitis and hypertension are common comorbidities in elderly patients with a history of smoking.
Radiation therapy for prostate cancer can have long-term effects on surrounding tissues.

required.content: What were the findings from the patient's recent follow-up examinations?
required.response: A CT scan showed a cyst in the right kidney, no lymphadenopathy, and minimal periprostatic and perirectal stranding. A radionuclide bone scan showed an isolated focus of increased activity in the right femur.

teaching_points.content: Cysts in the kidney are often benign but require monitoring for changes.
Bone scans can help differentiate between metastatic disease and other causes of bone lesions.

required.content: What symptoms did the patient experience before admission?
required.response: Two months before admission, the patient began to have swelling of the left leg and pain in the left groin that radiated down the entire leg.

teaching_points.content: Swelling and pain in the leg can indicate vascular issues such as aneurysms or deep vein thrombosis.

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Contained Ruptured Femoral Artery Aneurysm
key_features: pain in the left groin radiating down the leg
supporting_evidence: diagnosis of contained ruptured aneurysm of the left femoral artery
swelling and pain in the left leg
additional_information_needed: Details of imaging studies confirming the aneurysm

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT)
additional_information_needed: Doppler ultrasound of the left leg

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Metastatic Bone Disease
key_features: history of prostate and colon cancer
supporting_evidence: history of prostate and colon cancer
isolated focus of increased activity in the right femur
refuting_evidence: no direct evidence of metastasis causing current symptoms
additional_information_needed: Biopsy of the femoral lesion if indicated

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Mesothelioma
refuting_evidence: no imaging evidence of pleural disease

required.content: What were the findings on physical examination upon admission?
required.response: The patient appeared well, with normal head, neck, lungs, and heart. There was +++ pitting edema of the left lower extremity, a prominent left femoral pulse, and absent dorsalis pedis pulse on the left.

teaching_points.content: Pitting edema and changes in pulse can indicate vascular compromise.

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Peripheral Arterial Disease (PAD) with possible acute limb ischemia
supporting_evidence: absent dorsalis pedis pulse on the left
pain in the left groin radiating down the leg
additional_information_needed: Doppler ultrasound of the lower extremities

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT)
supporting_evidence: pain in the left groin radiating down the leg
refuting_evidence: absent dorsalis pedis pulse suggests arterial rather than venous issue
additional_information_needed: Venous Doppler ultrasound of the left leg

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Aneurysm of the left femoral artery
supporting_evidence: diagnosis of a contained, ruptured aneurysm of the left femoral artery
refuting_evidence: absent dorsalis pedis pulse suggests possible embolization or thrombosis
additional_information_needed: CT angiography of the lower extremities

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Metastatic bone disease
key_features: history of prostate and colon cancer
supporting_evidence: history of stage B1 carcinoma of the prostate
history of carcinoma of the colon
isolated focus of increased activity in the right femur on bone scan
refuting_evidence: no direct evidence of bone pain or fracture in the left leg
additional_information_needed: Biopsy of the right femur lesion
Further imaging studies to assess for metastasis

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Chronic venous insufficiency
supporting_evidence: +++ pitting edema of the left lower extremity
refuting_evidence: absent dorsalis pedis pulse suggests arterial issue

required.content: What were the results of the CT scan and other imaging studies?
required.response: CT scan showed a poorly defined soft-tissue density surrounding the left external iliac artery, with scattered calcifications and a maximal diameter of 2 cm. Aortographic and angiographic studies showed a diffuse, irregular aneurysm involving multiple arteries.

teaching_points.content: Imaging studies are crucial for diagnosing and assessing the extent of vascular aneurysms.

required.content: What were the laboratory test results?
required.response: The urine, complete blood count, prothrombin time, partial-thromboplastin time, urea nitrogen, creatinine, glucose, electrolytes, calcium, phosphorus, serum aspartate aminotransferase, amylase, and alkaline phosphatase were normal.

teaching_points.content: Normal laboratory results can help rule out systemic causes of symptoms.

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Peripheral Artery Disease (PAD) with Aneurysm
supporting_evidence: pain in the left groin radiating down the leg
absent dorsalis pedis pulse on the left
additional_information_needed: Doppler ultrasound of the lower extremities

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT)
supporting_evidence: pain in the left groin radiating down the leg
refuting_evidence: absent dorsalis pedis pulse suggests arterial rather than venous issue
additional_information_needed: Venous Doppler ultrasound of the left leg

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Metastatic Prostate Cancer
supporting_evidence: history of stage B1 carcinoma of the prostate
isolated focus of increased activity in the right femur on bone scan
additional_information_needed: Biopsy of the right femur lesion if clinically indicated

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Mesothelioma
additional_information_needed: Pleural biopsy if pleural abnormalities are found

required.content: What management decisions were made for the patient's condition?
required.response: A diagnostic procedure was performed, but specific management decisions are not detailed in the case.

teaching_points.content: Management of vascular aneurysms often involves surgical intervention or endovascular repair.

final_diagnosis.name: Contained Ruptured Aneurysm of the Left Femoral Artery
key_features: Swelling and pain in the left leg
